entry: Seasonal state of minimal activity and reduced metabolism, entered by some animals to pass through the [[Winter|winter]] months. Hibernation is a form of heterothermy in which body temperature, breathing and heart rate are lowered, so that the animal conserves energy when sufficient food is unavailable. Before entering dormancy, animals must store enough energy to last the entire period: larger species become hyperphagic and build fat deposits, while many small species cache food instead. Some [[Mammal|mammals]] hibernate while pregnant; female [[Bear|bears]] give birth during or shortly after the dormancy. Although the term was traditionally reserved for deep hibernators such as [[Rodent|rodents]], it is now applied according to metabolic suppression rather than an absolute drop in body temperature. The summer equivalent is aestivation.

Genus of plants in the family Malvaceae, native to the tropics and subtropics. The genus comprises 319 species of annual or perennial herbs, [[Shrub|shrubs]] and small trees. It is known for its large, showy [[Flower|flowers]], which are trumpet-shaped, with five or more petals, in colors from white to pink, red, blue, orange and peach. Several species are widely cultivated as ornamental plants. The genus was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. Its species are native to regions from China to East Africa and [[Hawaii]].

Common name for trees of the genus Carya, in the walnut family (Juglandaceae). The genus includes 19 species: seven native to Southeast Asia and twelve to North America. Hickories are temperate to subtropical forest [[Tree|trees]] with pinnately compound leaves and large [[Nut (fruit)|nuts]]. Most species are deciduous, but one species in Southeast Asia is evergreen. The fruit is a single nut enclosed in a four-valved husk that splits open at maturity. The shell is thick and bony in most species, but thin in the [[Pecan|pecan]]. Early fossil nuts had simpler, thinner shells than modern species, suggesting that defenses against [[Rodent|rodent]] seed predation developed gradually. A number of species are used for their edible nuts or for their wood.

Children's game in which one player seeks others who have hidden. After the seeker counts to a predetermined number with eyes closed, the other players conceal themselves within the surrounding area. The game usually ends when the seeker has found all players: the first player found becomes the next seeker, and the last player found is the winner. An early attested version, called apodidraskinda in [[Ancient Greek]], was mentioned by the second-century Greek writer Julius Pollux. In a variant called [[Sardine|sardines]], only one person hides and the others join them when found, until the final seeker finds the crowded group. In the comic strip *Peanuts*, a sardines variant called Ha Ha Herman is played. The game requires children to use theory of mind and executive function, such as inhibiting the urge to peek.

Japanese army officer and prime minister of Japan, 1941–44. Born into a samurai family in [[Tokyo]], he graduated from the Imperial Japanese Army Academy in 1905. As chief of staff of the Kwantung Army, he led operations in the Japanese invasion of China in 1937, and as army minister he advocated a tripartite alliance with [[Nazi Germany]] and Fascist Italy. Appointed prime minister by [[Hirohito|Emperor Hirohito]] in October 1941, he promoted total mobilization for war, enforced strict censorship and oversaw the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|attack on Pearl Harbor]], which brought Japan into [[World War II]]. Japan's defeat at the [[Battle of Midway]] in June 1942 weakened his position, and he resigned in July 1944. Convicted by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East of war crimes and crimes against peace, he was sentenced to death and hanged.

Japanese video game designer, writer and director, best known for the *Metal Gear* franchise. He directed the original *Metal Gear* (1987) after joining Konami in 1986, and he continued to direct the series for 28 years, up to *Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain* (2015). He founded Kojima Productions within Konami in 2005. After leaving Konami in 2015, he re-established the studio as an independent company and, in partnership with [[Sony]], released *Death Stranding* (2019) and *Death Stranding 2: On the Beach* (2025).

Dutch painter from 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant, one of the most notable representatives of the Early Netherlandish school. Born Jheronimus van Aken, he was descended from a family with roots in Nijmegen and [[Aachen]] and spent most of his life in 's-Hertogenbosch, where little is known of his life beyond municipal and confraternity records. His fantastical religious paintings, generally oil on oak panel, depict moral and religious narratives, and his macabre images of [[Hell|hell]] were widely copied in his lifetime. Only about 25 paintings are confidently attributed to him, along with eight drawings. His most acclaimed works are three triptych altarpieces, particularly *The Garden of Earthly Delights*. [[Pieter Bruegel the Elder]] was his best-known follower.

Massive elementary particle in the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics, produced by quantum excitation of the Higgs field. The boson has zero spin and no electric or color charge, and it decays almost immediately into other particles. The Higgs field takes a nonzero value everywhere, giving rest mass to elementary particles through the Higgs mechanism, which Peter Higgs and five other scientists in three teams proposed in 1964. After a 40-year search, the particle was discovered in 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the [[Large Hadron Collider|Large Hadron Collider]] at [[CERN]] near [[Geneva]]. Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics in 2013. The particle has often been called the God particle in the media, a name that physicists, including Higgs, have criticized.

[[Track and field]] event in which competitors jump unaided over a horizontal bar set at measured heights. Alongside the [[Pole vault|pole vault]], it is one of two vertical clearance events in the Olympic athletics program. Competitors must take off from one foot, and a jump fails if the jumper dislodges the bar or touches the ground behind it. The preferred technique is the Fosbury flop, in which athletes run toward the bar and leap head first with their back to it. The high jump was among the first events deemed acceptable for women, having been held at the 1928 [[Olympic Games|Olympic Games]]. Javier Sotomayor of Cuba holds the men's world record of 2.45 m, set in 1993, and Yaroslava Mahuchikh of Ukraine holds the women's record of 2.10 m, set in 2024. Ties are broken by the fewest misses, and then by a jump-off.

Atmospheric region where air pressure is higher than in surrounding areas, also called an anticyclone. Highs are middle-scale features that result from interplay between larger patterns of atmospheric circulation. The strongest form when cold air from polar regions spreads into cooler neighboring regions, while more frequent weaker highs result from subsidence, in which cool, drier air descends. [[Wind|Winds]] flow outward from the center and are curved by the [[Coriolis force]], rotating clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern. High pressure typically brings clear skies, and in summer and winter it brings warm and cold weather respectively in temperate latitudes. On English-language [[Weather|weather]] maps, high-pressure centers are marked H. The term anticyclone was coined in 1877 by [[Francis Galton]].

Rail transport network using trains that run significantly faster than conventional trains on dedicated tracks. Lines are generally considered high-speed when built for at least 250 km/h (155 mph), or when upgraded lines run at least 200 km/h (125 mph). The first dedicated system, the Tōkaidō [[Shinkansen]] in [[Japan]], opened in October 1964; its streamlined nose gave the trains the nickname bullet train. European countries followed, starting with [[Italy]]'s Direttissima line and then [[France]], Germany and Spain. As of 2023, [[China]]'s network accounted for over two-thirds of the world's total. High-speed trains mostly run on standard gauge track. High-speed rail is the fastest and most efficient ground-based method of commercial transport, but its construction costs more than conventional rail and does not always offer an economic advantage.

Scottish breed of hardy cattle with long horns and a long shaggy coat, originating in the [[Scottish Highlands]] and the Western Islands of Scotland. The first herd book, published in 1885, recorded a smaller island type, usually black, and a larger mainland type, usually dun, as a single breed. Reared mainly for [[Beef|beef]], the breed has been exported to many countries, including the [[Falkland Islands]]. In 1954 [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] began keeping a herd at Balmoral Castle, where cattle are still kept. A group of Highland cattle is known as a fold.

Public road or other public way on land, in the broadest sense. In the United States the term usually denotes a major road, and it is often used as a synonym of freeway or of a [[Controlled-access highway|controlled-access highway]]. In North American and Australian English they are typically state highways, or provincial highways in Canada, reflecting the level of government that maintains them. In British English, highway is primarily a legal term covering any route with a public right of access, including footpaths. Highways were used first on foot or on horseback, and later accommodated carriages, [[Bicycle|bicycles]] and [[Car|motor cars]]. In the 1920s and 1930s many nations invested heavily in highway systems to spur commerce and bolster national defense. [[Australia]]'s Highway 1 is the longest national highway in the world, at over 14,500 km, and [[China]] has the world's largest network, followed closely by the United States.

Headscarf worn by many Muslim women, covering the hair, neck and ears. In Islamic literature the term also denotes an inner sense of modesty and reserve. The [[Quran|Qur'an]] mentions only khimār, usually rendered as headscarf, and jilbāb, an outer garment. Classical scholars argue that covering the head is a religious requirement, while modernist thinkers do not consider it an Islamic obligation. The hijab is mandated by law in [[Iran]] and under [[Taliban]] rule in [[Afghanistan]], while other countries restrict or ban it. Such regulations raise questions of women's participation in public life and [[Human rights|human rights]].

Long, vigorous walk, usually on [[Trail|trails]] or footpaths in the countryside, undertaken for recreation. Walking for pleasure developed in Europe during the eighteenth century, although long hikes as part of a religious [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] existed much earlier. In Canada and the United States hiking is the preferred term, while walking describes shorter urban walks; in the United Kingdom walking covers all forms of the activity. Multi-day hikes are called backpacking, and trekking describes multi-day hiking in mountainous regions. Hiking can involve bushwhacking through dense vegetation, where a [[Machete|machete]] may be needed to clear a path. The Italian poet [[Petrarch]] is often cited as an early recreational hiker after climbing Mont Ventoux on April 26, 1336, though some have suggested his account is fictional.

American actress and film producer. Swank won two Academy Awards for Best Actress, for her portrayal of Brandon Teena in *Boys Don't Cry* (1999) and for playing a female boxer in *Million Dollar Baby* (2004), directed by [[Clint Eastwood]]. Her other films include *Freedom Writers* (2007) and *Amelia* (2009). On television she played Alice Paul in the [[HBO]] film *Iron Jawed Angels* (2004). [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2005.

Set of 23 mathematical problems proposed by German mathematician [[David Hilbert]] in 1900. Hilbert intended to rival [[Henri Poincaré]], the master of French mathematics, and presented ten of the problems at the [[Paris]] conference of the International Congress of Mathematicians on August 8. The problems range from the cardinal number of the continuum to the axioms of physics. All were unsolved when published, and several proved highly influential for 20th-century mathematics. By consensus, ten of the cleanly formulated problems have accepted resolutions, while the eighth, the [[Riemann hypothesis]], remains unresolved. The fourth and twenty-third are considered too vague ever to be solved.

Type of vector space that generalizes Euclidean space to any finite or infinite dimension. A Hilbert space has an inner product that allows length and angle to be measured, and it is complete, so that enough limits exist for the techniques of calculus. It was studied from the first decade of the 20th century by [[David Hilbert]], Erhard Schmidt and Frigyes Riesz, and it is indispensable in [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]], [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], Fourier analysis and ergodic theory. [[John von Neumann]] coined the term for the abstract concept. Examples include spaces of square-integrable functions and of sequences. Exact analogs of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] hold, and perpendicular projection onto a subspace is central to optimization. These methods helped establish [[Functional analysis|functional analysis]] as a fruitful field.

German Benedictine abbess and [[Polymath|polymath]], known as the Sibyl of the Rhine. Elected magistra of her community at Disibodenberg in 1136, she founded the monasteries of Rupertsberg in 1150 and Eibingen in 1165. Her works include theological, medical and natural history writings, letters, poems, [[Hymn|hymns]] and the visionary *Scivias*. She has more surviving chants than any other composer of the [[Middle Ages]], and she is one of few known composers to have written both the music and the words of her works. Her *Ordo Virtutum* is arguably the oldest surviving morality play. Some scholars regard her as the founder of scientific natural history in Germany. On May 10, 2012, [[Pope Benedict XVI]] extended her liturgical cult to the entire [[Catholic Church]], and on October 7, 2012, he named her a Doctor of the Church.

Landform that extends above the surrounding terrain, often with a distinct summit, and not as prominent as a [[Mountain|mountain]]. The distinction between a hill and a mountain is subjective, but hills are universally considered less tall and less steep. Hills form through faulting, through [[Erosion|erosion]] of larger landforms, or through glacial deposition of sediment, such as [[Moraine|moraines]] and drumlins. Their rounded summits result from downhill creep, the slow movement of soil and regolith. Many settlements were built on hills to avoid floods or for defense; [[Ancient Rome]] was built on seven hills. Artificial hills are known as mounds or tumuli, and a hillock is a small hill.

American politician, lawyer and diplomat. She was first lady of the United States from 1993 to 2001, the 67th United States secretary of state under [[Barack Obama]] from 2009 to 2013, and a U.S. senator for New York from 2001 to 2009. She was the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] nominee in the 2016 presidential election, the first woman to win a major party's presidential nomination. She won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College to [[Donald Trump]]. Her use of a private email server as secretary of state drew intense scrutiny, although no charges were filed.

State in the Western [[Himalayas]] of northern India, whose name means snow-laden mountain province. It shares its eastern border with the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] of China. Shimla is the summer capital and Dharamshala the winter capital. Hilly areas of [[Punjab]] were merged into the state in 1966, and it was granted full statehood in 1971. Agriculture, horticulture, [[Hydropower|hydropower]] and tourism are important to the economy. Households are almost universally electrified, with 99.5% having electricity as of 2016, and the state has 12 districts.

Fire that destroyed the German [[Airship|airship]] Hindenburg (LZ 129) as it attempted to dock at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, in [[New Jersey]], on May 6, 1937. The [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]]-filled airship burned quickly, killing 35 of the 97 people on board and one person on the ground. Newsreel coverage and Herbert Morrison's radio reports, broadcast the next day, made the disaster widely known. Several theories have been advanced for the cause of ignition, including [[Static electricity|static electricity]]. The publicity shattered public confidence in large passenger airships and marked the abrupt end of the airship era.

Modern Standard Hindi, an Indo-Aryan language written in the [[Devanagari]] script. It is an official language of [[India]] and, with English, serves as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] across much of northern, central, eastern, western and northeastern India. Standard Hindi is mutually intelligible with standard [[Urdu]], and the common base of the two is called [[Hindustani language|Hindustani]]. Hindi is the fourth-most-spoken first language in the world, after Mandarin, Spanish and English. Like other Indo-Aryan languages, it descends from an early form of [[Sanskrit]], and its direct ancestors emerged in the 7th century CE. The word Hindi derives from Persian, meaning of or belonging to Hind (India).

Base-ten positional numeral system, the most common system for writing numbers. It uses ten glyphs, from zero to nine, to represent any natural number as a unique sequence. Indian mathematicians invented it between the 1st and 4th centuries, and Arabic mathematicians adopted it in the 9th century, extending it to fractions. [[Al-Khwarizmi|Al-Khwārizmī]] and [[Al-Kindi]] wrote about it in Arabic, and [[Fibonacci|Fibonacci]]'s 13th-century Liber Abaci helped it reach Europe, where until the [[Printing press|printing press]] in the 15th century its use was mainly confined to Northern Italy.
